label: rem1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem1} In the cases of $\alpha=1 \  \textrm{and}  \ \alpha=0 $ the $\alpha$-p differential
transform (\ref{dtmm25}) reduces to the classical differential
transform (\ref{dtm2}) at the points  $x=a \  \textrm{and}  \ x=b $
respectively. Namely for $\alpha=0 \  \textrm{and}  \ \alpha=1 $ the
equality $\widetilde{f_{\alpha}}(x)=f(x)$ is hold.
head: environment

title: Remark

label: rem11
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{rem11} If f(x) is constant function then
$\widetilde{f_{\alpha}}(x)=f(x)$ and
$\widetilde{f}_{\alpha,N}(x)=f(x)$ for each $N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is immediate from Definition \ref{dfnn} and
Remark \ref{remn1}.
head: environment

label: dtm11
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{dtm11}
By applying the well-known properties of classical DTM we get
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{dtm12}
D(f,\alpha;k)&=&\alpha D_{a}(f;k) +(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(f;k)\nonumber\\&=&\alpha c  D_{a}(g;k)+(1-\alpha)c D_{b}(g;k)
\nonumber\\&=&c(\alpha   D_{a}(g;k)+(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(g;k))\nonumber\\&=&c D(g,\alpha;k)
\end{eqnarray}
Consequently $D_{\alpha}(f)=c D_{\alpha}(g)$, from which immediately
follows that $\widetilde{f_{\alpha}}(x)=c
\widetilde{g_{\alpha}}(x)$.
head: environment

label: dtm9
title: Proof
body_md:
By using the definition of transform (\ref{dtmm25})
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{dtm9}
D(f,\alpha;k)&=&\alpha D_{a}(f;k)\pm(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(f;k)\nonumber\\&=&\alpha D_{a}(g+h;k)\pm(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(g+h;k)\nonumber\\&=& D(g,\alpha;k)\pm D(h,\alpha;k)
\end{eqnarray}
Consequently $D_{\alpha}(f)=D_{\alpha}(g)\pm D_{\alpha}(h)$, from
which immediately follows that $ \widetilde{f_{\alpha}}(x)=
\widetilde{g}_{\alpha}(x)\pm \widetilde{h}_{\alpha}(x)$.
head: environment

label: dtm13
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dtm13}
Let  $f(x)=\frac{d^{m}g}{dx^{m}}$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}$. Then
$$D(f^{(m)},\alpha;k)=\frac{(k+m)!}{k!}D(f,\alpha;k+m)$$ and
$$\widetilde{f}_{\alpha}^{(m)}(x)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(k+m)!}{k!}D(f,\alpha;k+m)(x-x_{\alpha})^{k}$$
where  $x_{\alpha}=\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b$.
head: environment

label: dtm14
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{dtm14}We have from definition (\ref{dtmm25})
 \begin{eqnarray*}\label{dtm15}
D(f^{(m)},\alpha;k)&=&\alpha D_{a}(f^{(m)};k)+(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(f^{(m)};k)\nonumber\\&=&\alpha (k+1)(k+2)...(k+m)
D_{a}(f;k+m)\nonumber\\&+&(1-\alpha)(k+1)(k+2)...(k+m)
D_{b}(f;k+m)\nonumber\\&=&(k+1)(k+2)...(k+m)(\alpha
D_{a}(f;k)+(1-\alpha)D_{b}(f;k+m))\nonumber\\&=&\frac{(k+m)!}{k!}D(f,\alpha;k+m)
\end{eqnarray*}
Thus we get $D(f^{(m)},\alpha;k)=\frac{(k+m)!}{k!}D(f,\alpha;k+m)$.
Using this we find
$\widetilde{f}_{\alpha}^{(m)}(x)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(k+m)!}{k!}D(f,\alpha;k+m)(x-x_{\alpha})^{k}$.
head: environment

label: dtm17
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{dtm17} Let $ k<m$. By using the definition of the transform
(\ref{dtmm25}) we have
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{dtm18}
D(f,\alpha;k)&=&\alpha D_{a}(f;k)+(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(f;k)\nonumber\\&=&\alpha D_{a}(x^{(m)};k)+(1-\alpha)
D_{b}(x^{(m)};k)\nonumber\\&=&\left( 
\begin{array}{c}
  m \\
  k \\
\end{array} 
\right)(\alpha a^{(m-k)}+(1-\alpha)b^{(m-k)})
\end{eqnarray}
 The equalities $\ D(x^{m},\alpha;m)=1 $ and $\
D(x^{m},\alpha;m+s)=0$ for $s\geq1$ is obvious.
